title: India's Services Sector Just Had Its Best Month Since November. The Jobs Data Tells a Different Story.
excerpt: HSBC's India Services PMI rose to 59.8 in May, the highest in six months, on a surge in domestic demand. But fewer than 7 percent of firms are actually hiring.
body:
India's dominant services sector expanded at its fastest pace in six months in May, driven by a sharp pick-up in domestic demand from e-commerce, entertainment, and IT. But beneath the headline strength, the data reveals a labour market that is struggling to keep up with output growth and a business confidence gauge that has now slipped for two consecutive months.

HSBC's India Services Purchasing Managers' Index, compiled by S&P Global, rose to 59.8 in May from 58.8 in April, comfortably beating a preliminary estimate of 58.9. Any reading above 50 indicates expansion, and India's services PMI has stayed above that threshold continuously since mid-2021 — one of the longest unbroken expansion streaks of any major economy.

## Demand Is Surging, But Not From Abroad

New business orders — the core gauge of demand — climbed to their highest since November 2025, led by domestic consumers rather than overseas clients. Export orders grew only slightly after touching a five-month low in April, with uncertainty over a pending U.S. trade deal suppressing international demand.

The sectoral drivers were telling. E-commerce, entertainment, and IT services led the expansion, reflecting a consumer economy that is spending on digital services and experiences even as inflation in food and fuel cuts into household budgets. But the recovery in IT is tentative — the sector has been hammered by concerns over AI-driven disruption, with the Nifty IT index down 22.4 percent for the year.

## The Hiring Gap

The most striking divergence in the May data is between output and employment. Despite headline PMI readings near 60 — territory that in developed economies would signal rapid hiring — fewer than 7 percent of the firms surveyed reported new recruitment. Services companies are producing more with existing staff, a pattern consistent with India's broader challenge of jobless growth.

This is not a new problem, but the scale of the gap is widening. A services sector posting a 59.8 PMI while generating minimal net new jobs suggests that productivity gains, automation, and the substitution of permanent roles with contract and gig work are accelerating faster than the expansion can absorb.

## Costs Are Easing, but Confidence Is Not

On the price side, the data offered some relief. Input cost inflation retreated for a second month from a 45-month high hit in March, giving firms breathing room to reduce prices charged to customers. The prices-charged sub-index fell to a four-month low — a small but meaningful signal in an economy where the RBI is weighing the risk of higher rates on Friday.

But the business outlook index slipped to 61.9 from 62.3, its second consecutive monthly decline. It now sits below its historical average, suggesting that services firms are growing more cautious even as demand improves. The Iran war's disruption to global energy supplies, the delayed monsoon, and the ongoing uncertainty over U.S.-India trade talks are all weighing on sentiment.

## The Composite Picture

The broader private sector economy also gained momentum. The Composite PMI — which combines services and manufacturing — rose to 59.3 in May from 58.2, its highest in six months. India's manufacturing PMI had already printed at 55 earlier this week, confirming that both halves of the economy are in solid expansion territory.

But the same tension runs through both datasets. Output is strong. Hiring is weak. Costs are moderating from peaks but remain elevated. And confidence is declining even as headline numbers improve. The economy is growing, but it is growing warily — with one eye on Friday's RBI decision, one eye on the Gulf, and both hands gripping what it already has.

*Sources: Reuters, S&P Global, HSBC India PMI Report*
author: Diaspora Desk
